chapter: Childhood in Oklahoma, Kansas City and Tulsa
title: Oklahoma bands of the early 1930s: Ernie Fields and the trumpeter Fred Skinner
summary: Back in Oklahoma in 1929 he hears Trent, Love and Holder, and the local Ernie Fields band with its high-note trumpeter Skinner, who died of pneumonia.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: Then, we went back to Oklahoma in '29. And these same bands was coming through Oklahoma. And when I got to Oklahoma, I ran into the bands of Alphonso Trent, Clyde Love, no, Clarence Love, what's this other -- Tee Holder. And the local bands, which was two, one and two -- of course, there were others, but the number one band was Ernie Fields. And he had a trumpet player with him then -- this was like '31. And this kid was 21, and his father was a bandmaster and had a band of his own. His name was Fred Skinner. And he had taught his son trumpet. And he played high notes like Cat Anderson does today. And his (laughs) horn was taped up with tape, gum. However, he died an early death. He was in Dakota, Deadwood, North Dakota. And it was very cold, and he was wearing long johns. And he washed them out that night, and he had to leave before they dried out. And he put them back on, and got what I guess they call lobar pneumonia. Died overnight.
Who were you acquainted with in the bands? Were you acquainted with any of the members of the bands?
Yes, but his name rang out the most. I don't have a total recall of -- yes, there was a Basil Stone, a trumpet player, who turned out to be a preacher in St. Louis,
In the same band that Dart Skinner, Ned Skinner's son, the one that played the high notes, and -- let's see, they had a tenor

player, I think. They called him "Big Stack." I never knew his real name. And a couple of other fellows. I know their name, but I can't call them. I'm having a mental block. I can see them, but I can't call it.

All right. They had another band there called Al Denny, like, he took the jobs that Ernie Fields wasn't able to fulfill. You know, he was otherwise engaged. And then we had a school band that was out of sight. It was the Rhythm Aces. And then there was a band out of -- the Young band, the Grey Brothers. One of them years later married [Leomin] Lewis, who was a pianist and sang. She was a single.
